entities.summary:
The Pacific Ocean is the largest and deepest of Earth's five oceanic divisions, spanning over 155.6 million square kilometers and covering approximately 46% of the planet's water surface. Born out of the supercontinent of Pangaea during the break-up of the supercontinent in the Jurassic period, the Pacific Ocean played a pivotal role in the formation of Asia and the Americas, shaping the course of geological history and the distribution of life on Earth.

The Pacific Ocean is home to some of the most extreme and unique environments on the planet, including the Mariana Trench, the deepest point on Earth, and the Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system. The ocean's vast array of marine life, including blue whales, humpback whales, and sea turtles, has been the subject of intense scientific study and conservation efforts.

The Pacific Ocean has also played a significant role in human history, with many civilizations rising and falling along its shores. From the ancient Polynesian navigators who traversed the vast expanse of the Pacific in canoes, to the European explorers who mapped the ocean's shores and claimed its riches, the Pacific has been a hub of human activity and cultural exchange.


The Pacific Ocean continues to shape the world we live in today, with its waves and tides influencing the weather patterns and coastlines of the surrounding continents. As the world's largest ecosystem, the Pacific Ocean plays a critical role in regulating the Earth's climate and providing a source of food, energy, and livelihood for millions of people around the world.
